item.title: Claude Code Cron Job Setup: Run Automations Overnight
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Claude Code cron job setup: auth tokens, PATH, working directory, permissions, locks and log rotation, so overnight claude -p runs don't fail silently.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To set up a Claude Code cron job, you need two pieces. The first is a wrapper script that sets PATH, loads a token, cds into your project and runs claude -p with explicit permissions and limits. The second is one crontab line that runs that script under a lock and sends its output to a log file. Most "silent" overnight failures come from what cron does not give you: your shell's environment, your login, your project directory and a place to see errors. This guide covers each of those gaps, plus the scheduling options Anthropic offers if you don't want to manage cron yourself.

Should you use cron, or a built-in Claude Code scheduler?

Use cron when the job needs your machine's local files and tools and you want full control. Use Anthropic's built-in options when you'd rather not maintain a server. Claude Code now has three of its own scheduling options, and the official comparison shows how they differ:

OptionRuns onMachine must be onLocal filesMinimum intervalMain limitation
System cron + claude -pYour machine/serverYesYes1 minute (cron)You handle auth, env, logs, locking
Routines (cloud)Anthropic cloudNoNo (fresh clone)1 hourResearch preview; GitHub repos only
Desktop scheduled tasksYour machineYes, app open and awakeYes1 minuteSkipped while the computer sleeps
/loopYour open sessionYesYes1 minuteSession-scoped, expires after 7 days

How to choose:

  • Routines suit you if your work lives in GitHub and should run while your laptop is closed. They're available on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans (source, as of October 2026). Not for you if the job needs files outside a repo, local databases, or tools you can't install from a setup script. The docs also note that routines are in research preview and that a green run status "does not mean the task in your prompt succeeded" (source).
  • Desktop scheduled tasks suit people who keep the Claude Desktop app open on a work machine. Not for you if the machine sleeps overnight. If it sleeps through a scheduled time, the run is skipped, and on wake only one catch-up run happens (source).
  • /loop is for polling during a session you have open. Recurring tasks expire seven days after you create them (source), so it can't replace cron.
  • Cron fits an always-on Linux box, VPS or home server where you want plain files, plain logs and no extra platform.

The rest of this guide is about the cron route.

Trap 1: authentication that works in your terminal but not in cron

Your cron job needs a credential passed in explicitly through an environment variable, because the login in your interactive terminal may not reach it. Claude Code's authentication docs list two common options for scripts:

  • Subscription token: run claude setup-token once. It opens the browser flow and prints a one-year OAuth token without saving it anywhere. Set that token as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. It requires a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan (source, as of October 2026), and it can only make model requests, so claude.ai connectors won't work with it.
  • API key: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to a key from the Claude Console. Usage is billed to your API account instead of your subscription. In -p mode, the key "is always used when present" (source).

Two details often cause trouble:

  1. Precedence. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ranks above CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (source). If both exist, you are billed through the API key, which may not be what you intended.
  2. --bare ignores the OAuth token. Bare mode is recommended for scripts, but it "does not read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN". With --bare, use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper instead (source).

Why this fails silently: when a failure happens inside the run, "such as missing authentication, Claude Code prints the failure as the result on stdout" (source). If you throw stdout away, the error disappears with it. Check the exit code too: Claude Code exits with a non-zero code when a run fails.

Trap 2: PATH and the minimal cron environment

Cron runs your command in a much smaller environment than your terminal, so set every variable the job needs inside the script itself. The crontab(5) man page says cron sets SHELL to /bin/sh and takes LOGNAME and HOME from /etc/passwd. Anything your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc adds is not guaranteed to be there.

That matters for Claude Code because the native installer puts the launcher at ~/.local/bin/claude (source), and that directory is often added to PATH only by your shell profile. The tools Claude calls during the run also need to be found: node, git, gh, npm and so on.

Practical fixes:

  • Use the absolute path to claude (run which claude in your terminal to find it), or export a full PATH at the top of the script.
  • Keep secrets in a dedicated env file with chmod 600, and load it in the script. Don't paste them into the crontab.
  • Watch for % in crontab lines. Unless escaped, cron turns it into a newline and sends the rest of the line to standard input (source). That breaks date +%F inline, so put date formatting in the script.
  • Cron uses the system timezone unless you set CRON_TZ (on cron implementations that support it, such as cronie, per the crontab(5) man page).

Trap 3: the working directory decides what Claude loads

Always cd into the project explicitly, because the folder a -p run starts in decides which configuration and instructions it loads. Without --bare, claude -p "loads the same context an interactive session would, including anything configured in the working directory or ~/.claude". That includes CLAUDE.md, the hooks in .claude/settings.json and the MCP servers in .mcp.json (source).

Two consequences:

  • Wrong directory, wrong behavior. If the job starts somewhere else, Claude won't see your project's CLAUDE.md or settings, and relative paths in your prompt point to the wrong files.
  • No trust dialog. A -p session "shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt", so project hooks and MCP servers run even in a folder you've never trusted (source). Only point cron at repositories you control.

If you want the same result on every run no matter what's in ~/.claude, use --bare and pass context explicitly with --append-system-prompt-file, --settings and --mcp-config (source). The trade-off is that you then need an API key (see Trap 1).

Trap 4: permissions in a run nobody is watching

Set the permission mode and the allowed tools explicitly, because no one is awake to answer a prompt. The docs warn that a run with no permission mode set takes a built-in starting mode, "which can be auto, so pass the one you want" (source).

Options from the headless docs and the CLI reference:

  • --permission-mode dontAsk denies anything that would prompt, while reads and your --allowedTools entries still run. This is a good default for locked-down jobs.
  • --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test )" grants narrow, prefix-matched commands. The space before matters: Bash(git diff*) would also match git diff-index.
  • --permission-prompts none tells Claude that nobody can approve requests and not to retry denied ones. It requires v2.1.259 or later.
  • --max-turns caps agentic turns. There is no limit by default.
  • --max-budget-usd stops the run at an estimated spend. It's a client-side estimate, and spend can go past the cap, so leave headroom.

Avoid --dangerously-skip-permissions for overnight jobs unless the machine is a disposable sandbox.

Putting it together: script, crontab, lock and log rotation

The setup has four parts: a wrapper script, a crontab line with flock, structured logs, and rotation so the logs don't fill your disk. Everything below is an example. Change the paths, prompt and tool list to fit your project.

Step 1: the wrapper script

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ~/bin/claude-nightly.sh  (example)
set -uo pipefail

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"
set -a; source "$HOME/.config/claude-cron/env"; set +a   # holds CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=...
unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY   # avoid accidental precedence over the token

cd "$HOME/projects/myapp" || { echo "cd failed"; exit 1; }

LOG_DIR="$HOME/logs/claude-cron"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
STAMP=$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M)
OUT="$LOG_DIR/run-$STAMP.json"

claude -p "$(cat .claude/nightly-prompt.md)" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --permission-prompts none \
  --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *),Bash(git status *),Bash(git diff *)" \
  --max-turns 30 \
  --max-budget-usd 3 \
  --output-format json > "$OUT" 2> "$LOG_DIR/run-$STAMP.err"
STATUS=$?

echo "$(date -Is) exit=$STATUS cost=$(jq -r '.total_cost_usd // "n/a"' "$OUT" 2>/dev/null)"
[ "$STATUS" -eq 0 ] || echo "FAILED: $(jq -r '.result // empty' "$OUT" 2>/dev/null | head -c 500)"
exit "$STATUS"

Why these choices: --output-format json gives you result, session_id and total_cost_usd in a form a script can parse (source). Branching on the exit code catches failed runs. Keeping the prompt in a file means you can version-control it.

Step 2: the crontab line

Run crontab -e:

SHELL=/bin/bash
MAILTO=""
7 2 * * * /usr/bin/flock -n /tmp/claude-nightly.lock $HOME/bin/claude-nightly.sh >> $HOME/logs/claude-cron/cron.log 2>&1

flock -n makes the job "fail rather than wait if the lock cannot be immediately acquired" (flock(1)). If last night's run is still going, a second copy won't start on top of it. Cron mails command output to the crontab owner or to MAILTO (cron(8)). Since this setup sends output to a file, set MAILTO="" so cron doesn't also try to send mail.

Step 3: log rotation

Rotate the summary log with logrotate, and prune the per-run files with find. An example /etc/logrotate.d/claude-cron:

/home/you/logs/claude-cron/cron.log {
    weekly
    rotate 8
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate
}

copytruncate truncates the file in place after copying it, so the >> in your crontab keeps writing to the same file. missingok and notifempty skip missing or empty logs (logrotate(8)). For the per-run JSON files, add a second cron line such as 0 4 0 find $HOME/logs/claude-cron -name 'run-*' -mtime +30 -delete.

Claude Code also saves session transcripts on disk. If you never resume these runs, --no-session-persistence stops them from being saved (source).

Step 4: test it under cron conditions

Before you trust the schedule, run the script in an environment as bare as cron's: env -i HOME="$HOME" /bin/sh -c '$HOME/bin/claude-nightly.sh'. Then schedule it a few minutes ahead and read cron.log and the JSON file. Also run claude auth status inside the script once: it reports which authMethod is active and exits 1 if you're not logged in (source).

Keeping overnight jobs healthy over time

Plan for updates, token expiry and alerting from the start, because these cause failures weeks after setup rather than on day one.

  • Updates: native installs update automatically in the background (source). If you want a predictable version for scheduled jobs, set "autoUpdatesChannel": "stable", or set DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 in your settings and update yourself.
  • Token expiry: the setup-token token lasts one year (source). Put a renewal reminder in your calendar.
  • Alerting: a failing exit code that only reaches a log file is still silent. For example, you could add a line to the script that sends the FAILED: message to a Slack webhook or a health-check service when the run fails.
  • Read the output, not just the status: as with routines, a clean exit means the process finished, not that the task was done well. Check the result text now and then.

FAQ

Can Claude Code run on a schedule without my computer on?

Yes, through Routines, which run on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure on hourly, nightly or weekly schedules (source). They work from a fresh clone of your GitHub repositories, so they can't see local files. The minimum interval is one hour, and the feature is in research preview.

Why does my Claude Code cron job work manually but not from cron?

Usually cron's environment is missing something your terminal has: ~/.local/bin on PATH, an exported token, or the project directory. Use absolute paths, load credentials from a file, and cd explicitly. Capture stdout, because Claude Code prints failures such as missing authentication there (source).

Should I use CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for cron?

Use CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token) if you want runs to count against your Claude subscription. Use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you want API billing, or if you run with --bare, which ignores the OAuth token (source). Don't set both, because the API key takes precedence.

How do I stop a scheduled Claude run from costing too much?

Combine --max-turns with --max-budget-usd, and log total_cost_usd from the JSON output. The budget cap uses a client-side estimate and spend can go past it, so set it below your real limit (source).

How do I prevent overlapping Claude cron runs?

Wrap the command in flock -n with a lock file. A new run then exits right away if the previous one still holds the lock (flock(1)).

Sources

  • Run Claude Code programmatically (headless) – Claude Code Docs
  • CLI reference – Claude Code Docs
  • Authentication – Claude Code Docs
  • Advanced setup – Claude Code Docs
  • Run prompts on a schedule – Claude Code Docs
  • Automate work with routines – Claude Code Docs
  • Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Code Desktop – Claude Code Docs
  • crontab(5) – Linux manual page
  • cron(8) – Debian manpages
  • flock(1) – Linux manual page
  • logrotate(8) – Linux manual page

item.title: Claude Code Checkpoints: How Rollback Works in Automations
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How Claude Code checkpoints work in headless jobs: enable SDK file checkpointing, save UUIDs, rewind unattended runs, and learn what rewind can't undo.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

In interactive Claude Code, checkpoints are on by default, and you undo with /rewind or by pressing Esc twice when the prompt is empty. Headless runs (claude -p or the Agent SDK) have nobody to press that key. You have to turn file checkpointing on, save the first user-message UUID and the session ID, and have your script call rewindFiles() / rewind_files() or run claude -p --resume <session-id> --rewind-files <checkpoint-uuid>. Rewind only restores edits made with Write, Edit and NotebookEdit. It doesn't cover Bash, most subagent edits or directories, so git stays your main safety net.

Which option is right for you?

Your setup depends on what the job does: rewind fully covers only jobs that edit files through Claude's own edit tools.

Your unattended job mostly…Main safety netRole of checkpoint rewind
Edits files (refactors, doc updates, lint fixes made with Edit/Write)Rewind, with a git commit underneathPrimary undo. Fast, and it can go back to a middle turn
Runs shell commands that change files (formatters, codemods, npm install, sed -i, mv)git, or a worktree you can throw awayPartial at best. Bash changes are not tracked
Uses subagents or background forked skillsgit, or a worktreeAssume it won't restore their edits
Touches things outside the repo (APIs, databases, deploys)Permission limits and dry runsNone. Rewind only covers local files

If you're not sure, start every run on a clean git commit or in a worktree, and treat rewind as a convenience on top.

A detail people often miss: --permission-mode acceptEdits also auto-approves common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv and cp (Headless docs). Those run through Bash, so rewind can't undo them even in a job you thought "only edits files."

What a checkpoint is and what it isn't

A checkpoint is a snapshot of files Claude edited with its file tools. It is not a full backup of your working tree. In interactive mode, Claude Code takes one each time you send a prompt that starts a turn. It keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session and saves them with the conversation, so /rewind still works after you resume (Checkpointing docs). The rewind menu can restore code and conversation, only the conversation, or only the code. It can also summarize from or up to a chosen point (same source).

These limits matter more when nobody is watching:

  • Bash changes are not tracked. Rewind can't undo rm, mv, cp, sed -i or echo > file when they run through Bash (Checkpointing docs; SDK docs).
  • Subagent edits usually aren't restored. The only exception is a skill with context: fork that runs in the foreground. Forked skills run in the background by default, and you set background: false to run one in the foreground. For every other subagent, the docs say to revert with git (Checkpointing docs).
  • Directories aren't undone. Rewind deletes files Claude created and restores files it modified. It doesn't reverse creating, moving or deleting directories, and it doesn't track remote or network files (SDK docs).
  • Links and some other paths are skipped. Since v2.1.216, rewind skips symlinks, hard links, other non-regular files, files whose parent directory no longer resolves to where it was at checkpoint time, and files whose backup can't be read safely. RewindFilesResult.skippedLinks counts all of these. Before v2.1.216, rewind wrote and deleted through links (SDK docs).
  • Snapshots expire. By default, the retention sweep deletes a session's snapshots about 30 days after the session last saved one. After that, a rewind can fail with "No files were restored." To keep snapshots longer, set cleanupPeriodDays (Checkpointing docs; Settings reference).
  • Checkpoints don't replace version control. Anthropic describes them as "quick, session-level recovery" and recommends git for permanent history (Checkpointing docs).

The fileCheckpointingEnabled setting turns the interactive /rewind snapshots on or off. When it is unset, snapshots are on (Settings reference).

How headless checkpointing differs

In the Agent SDK, checkpointing is opt-in, and it takes two options (SDK docs):

PurposePythonTypeScript
Track file changesenable_file_checkpointing=TrueenableFileCheckpointing: true
Get checkpoint UUIDs in the streamextra_args={"replay-user-messages": None}extraArgs: { "replay-user-messages": null }

With both set, each user message in the response stream carries a uuid you can use as a restore point. Rewinding to the first user message's UUID returns tracked files to their original state. Rewinding files doesn't rewind the conversation, which stays as it was (SDK docs).

The official examples also set permission_mode="acceptEdits" so edits go through without a prompt (SDK docs). Always pass a permission mode explicitly. A -p run that sets none starts in a built-in default mode, and that default can be auto (Headless docs).

Pattern 1: Rewind inside the run when validation fails

Use this pattern when your script can tell during the run that something has gone wrong. Examples: a test command fails, a protected file changes, or the diff is much larger than expected.

The docs' "checkpoint before risky operations" pattern keeps a user-message UUID and calls rewind_files() as soon as your own condition is true, while the stream is still open (SDK docs). Here is a shortened Python version. should_revert() is a placeholder for your own check:

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    enable_file_checkpointing=True,
    permission_mode="acceptEdits",
    extra_args={"replay-user-messages": None},
)

first_checkpoint = None
async with ClaudeSDKClient(options) as client:
    await client.query("Update dependencies and fix type errors")
    async for message in client.receive_response():
        if isinstance(message, UserMessage) and message.uuid and not first_checkpoint:
            first_checkpoint = message.uuid
        if should_revert(message) and first_checkpoint:   # your own check
            await client.rewind_files(first_checkpoint)
            break

You need to make two decisions:

  1. Pick which checkpoint to rewind to. The docs' version overwrites its variable every turn, so it keeps only the latest checkpoint and undoes only the last step. An unattended job usually wants to throw away the whole attempt, so the example above keeps the first UUID. To keep some turns and undo others, store every UUID. The docs call this "Multiple restore points" (SDK docs).
  2. Call rewind before the loop ends. If you call rewindFiles() after you've finished iterating, you get "ProcessTransport is not ready for writing," because the connection closes when the loop completes (SDK docs).

Pattern 2: Record IDs now, rewind later

Use this pattern when you only find out a run was bad after it ends, for example when CI goes red an hour later or someone reviews the diff the next morning.

  1. Save checkpoint_id and session_id for every run. A small JSON log next to the job output is enough. The docs show how to capture session_id from the ResultMessage (SDK docs).
  2. Rewind later by resuming with an empty prompt. Open a new client with enable_file_checkpointing=True and resume=session_id, send "", and call rewind_files(checkpoint_id) inside the response loop (SDK docs).
  3. Or rewind from the shell, without SDK code:
CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING=true \
  claude -p --resume <session-id> --rewind-files <checkpoint-uuid>

--rewind-files doesn't appear in claude --help, but the CLI accepts it. When it works, it prints Files rewound to state at message <checkpoint-uuid> and exits without sending a prompt. Without the environment variable, the bare CLI fails with "File rewinding is not enabled" (SDK docs).

Run the rewind on the same machine that ran the job. Checkpoints belong to the session that created them (SDK docs), and the snapshots live in local Claude Code state (Checkpointing docs). --resume <id> can find a session in other projects on the same machine (CLI reference). Running the rewind from the original project directory is still the safest choice.

Let the run finish before you depend on its checkpoints. "No file checkpoint found" can mean the session wasn't properly completed (SDK docs), and a claude -p run stopped with SIGTERM leaves its current turn unfinished (Headless docs). If your supervisor has to stop a job, send SIGINT or call the SDK's interrupt() first, as the headless docs recommend.

Using only the CLI, without the SDK

You can do this from a shell script. --replay-user-messages requires both --input-format stream-json and --output-format stream-json. You can also give the session a known ID up front with --session-id <uuid> so you don't have to parse it from the output (CLI reference).

The SDK sets CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING internally only when checkpointing is enabled, and the bare CLI never sets it (SDK docs). "No file checkpoint found" can mean checkpointing was off on the original session, so the safe reading is to set the variable on the original run as well as on the rewind. The docs don't describe this CLI-only flow end to end, so this is an inference. Test it on a throwaway repo before you rely on it.

Here is an example launch. The headless page doesn't show the stream-json input message format, so check it against the Agent SDK docs before use:

SID=$(uuidgen | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')
echo '{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":"Fix lint errors in src/"}}' | \
CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING=true claude -p \
  --session-id "$SID" \
  --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --replay-user-messages --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  > run.jsonl
CHECKPOINT=$(jq -r 'select(.type=="user" and .uuid) | .uuid' run.jsonl | head -1)
echo "$SID $CHECKPOINT" >> agent-runs.log

Don't use --no-session-persistence on runs you might want to rewind. It stops the session from being saved to disk, so the session can't be resumed (CLI reference), and a later rewind depends on resuming.

Rewind vs. git vs. worktrees: which to use when

Use all of them together. Each one covers gaps the others leave.

MechanismCoversMissesBest for
Checkpoint rewindWrite/Edit/NotebookEdit changes to local files (SDK docs)Bash changes, most subagent edits, directories, links, network filesFast, precise undo of the agent's own edits, including going back to a middle turn
Git commit/branch before the runEverything in the repo that git tracksUntracked/ignored files unless you include them; anything outside the repoThe baseline you can always reset to
--worktree / -wRuns in an isolated worktree at <repo>/.claude/worktrees/<name> (CLI reference)Side effects outside the repo (APIs, databases)Recurring jobs that should never touch your main checkout
Permission limitsBlocks risky actions up front, e.g. --disallowedTools "Bash(rm *)", --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259+) (CLI reference; Headless docs)Mistakes made with allowed toolsKeeping the damage within what rewind and git can undo

How to decide:

  • If you need to undo a run days later, check that the snapshots are still there (about 30 days by default) and raise cleanupPeriodDays if needed (Checkpointing docs).
  • If the job runs where other people's settings could load (CI, shared machines), consider --bare. The docs recommend it for scripted calls. In bare mode Claude Code skips hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md from the host, and it needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY instead of a subscription login (Headless docs).

A practical setup checklist

  1. Start each run on a clean git state, or in a worktree with claude -w <name> (CLI reference).
  2. Turn on checkpointing (enableFileCheckpointing / enable_file_checkpointing, or the env var for the bare CLI) and replay-user-messages (SDK docs).
  3. Set the permission mode explicitly (Headless docs).
  4. Save the first user-message UUID and the session ID for every run.
  5. Limit runaway runs with --max-turns and --max-budget-usd, which work in print mode only. The budget cap uses a client-side cost estimate that can differ from your bill, and spend can go past it, so leave headroom (CLI reference).
  6. Add a validation step (tests, lint, diff-size check) and rewind automatically when it fails.
  7. After any rewind, run git status. Anything still changed came from Bash, a subagent or a skipped path. Reset it with git.
  8. Read skippedLinks in RewindFilesResult and alert when it isn't zero, because those files kept their current contents (SDK docs).

Troubleshooting quick reference

Most rewind failures come from a missing option on the original run or from calling rewind at the wrong time.

SymptomLikely causeFix
message.uuid missingreplay-user-messages not setAdd it to extraArgs / extra_args (SDK docs)
"No file checkpoint found for this message"Checkpointing was off on the original session, or the session didn't finishEnable it on the original run and let the session finish before resuming (same)
"File rewinding is not enabled"Bare CLI without the env var, or a resumed SDK session without the optionSet CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING=true, or enable the option on the resumed session (same)
"ProcessTransport is not ready for writing"Rewind called after the loop endedResume with an empty prompt, then rewind (same)
"No files were restored"Snapshots removed by retention cleanupRaise cleanupPeriodDays; use git for this run (Checkpointing docs)
Files changed after a "successful" rewindBash edits (including mv/cp allowed by acceptEdits), subagent edits, or skipped pathsgit status, then git checkout/git clean the leftovers
Options not recognizedOld SDKpip install --upgrade claude-agent-sdk or npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk@latest (SDK docs)

FAQ

Are checkpoints on by default in claude -p or the Agent SDK?

No. Interactive sessions take snapshots by default. In the Agent SDK you have to enable file checkpointing and replay-user-messages, and with the bare CLI you set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING=true (SDK docs).

Can I skip git if I use checkpoints?

No. Anthropic says checkpoints are for quick, session-level recovery and recommends git for permanent history. Rewind also misses Bash changes, most subagent edits and directory operations (Checkpointing docs).

Does rewinding files also rewind the conversation?

Not in the SDK. rewindFiles() / rewind_files() restores files on disk and leaves the conversation history as it was. The interactive /rewind menu lets you choose code, conversation, or both (SDK docs; Checkpointing docs).

How long can I wait before rewinding a run?

By default, about 30 days after the session last saved a snapshot. After that, cleanup can remove the snapshots. You can change this with cleanupPeriodDays (Checkpointing docs).

Can I rewind on a different machine, such as a fresh CI runner?

Not reliably. Checkpoints are tied to the session that created them, and the snapshots live in local Claude Code state (SDK docs; Checkpointing docs). On short-lived runners, rely on git or worktrees instead.

Next steps

Pick the job type that matches your automation and try only the checklist items for that type today. Each list takes one throwaway repo and one run.

If your job mostly edits files (Edit/Write):

  1. Copy the Pattern 1 code. Replace should_revert() with one check, such as "tests fail."
  2. Run it once on a throwaway repo. Make the check fail on purpose and confirm the files go back.
  3. Run git status afterwards. If something is still changed, find which command caused it.

If your job mostly runs Bash commands:

  1. Wrap the run in claude -w <name>, or commit before each run.
  2. Write a one-line revert script: git reset --hard && git clean -fd, run inside the worktree only.
  3. Add --disallowedTools "Bash(rm *)" and --max-turns, then do one test run.

If your job uses subagents or forked skills:

  1. Assume rewind won't restore their edits, and run the job in a worktree.
  2. Save the session ID and first UUID anyway (Pattern 2), so the main agent's own edits can still be rewound.
  3. After a test run, compare git diff with the rewind result to see what the subagents changed.

If you'd rather not build this yourself: a freelance developer who knows the Agent SDK and your CI can usually set up a worktree, validation and revert script for you. You pay for their time on top of your usual Claude usage. Ask for a fixed-scope quote, because rates vary too much to give a reliable figure here. This suits you if you have one important recurring job and little time. It's a poor fit if your jobs change every week, because you'll keep paying for changes. Another route is to run the job in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI with Claude Code (GitHub Actions docs, GitLab CI/CD docs). Every run then starts from a clean checkout, and you undo it by not merging its branch, so you don't depend on checkpoints at all.

Related on Unattended: look for our guides on running claude -p on a schedule, choosing permission modes for unattended runs, and using git worktrees for agent jobs. They cover the layers that this article treats as "use git instead."

item.title: Why Claude Code Stops Mid-Automation (and How to Fix It)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Why does Claude Code stop running headless automations? Map the turn, budget, timeout and permission triggers in claude -p runs, plus a fix checklist.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A headless Claude Code run (claude -p) usually stops for one of three reasons. It reached a limit you set, such as --max-turns or --max-budget-usd. A timer ran out, such as the 2-minute Bash default, the 10-minute background-wait cap or your CI job's own timeout. Or it needed a permission that nobody was there to give, so the action was denied and Claude gave up on that step. The fix is to set each of these on purpose, read the result subtype and exit code after every run, and give the agent a clear, pre-approved set of tools.

This guide goes through each trigger using Anthropic's own documentation, then ends with a checklist you can copy into your scheduled jobs.

How to see why a run stopped

Before changing any settings, make every run report why it ended. Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails. One catch: when the failure happens inside the run (missing authentication, for example), the failure is printed as the result on stdout, not on stderr. If your cron script only logs stderr, you will miss it.

Use JSON output so you can read the result in your script:

claude -p "Triage new issues" --output-format json > run.json
jq -r '.subtype, .stop_reason, .total_cost_usd, .num_turns' run.json

The Agent SDK docs list these result subtypes: success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution and error_max_structured_output_retries. Every result includes total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id. The stop_reason field can also be max_tokens, which means the model hit its output token limit on the last turn.

For more detail, use --output-format stream-json --verbose. In that format, permission denials show up as permission_denied messages, and the final result lists them in permission_denials. Retryable API errors show up as system/api_retry events with a category such as rate_limit, overloaded, authentication_failed or max_output_tokens (source).

Trigger 1: Turn and token budgets

Max turns

--max-turns limits the number of agentic turns in print mode. It has no limit by default and exits with an error when the limit is reached. A turn is one tool-use round trip, so a task like "run tests, read files, edit, re-run tests" uses several. If you set --max-turns 3 to keep a nightly job small, it can stop before the edit step. The SDK docs give this same example, where max_turns=2 stops before the edit.

Fix: Give the job some room above the number of turns it normally needs, and treat error_max_turns as "resume later", not as a failure. The session ID still comes back, so you can run claude -p "continue" --resume "$session_id" (source).

Dollar budget

--max-budget-usd stops the run once estimated spend reaches the amount you set. Things to know:

  • The check uses a client-side cost estimate, which can differ from your bill.
  • Spend can go past the cap. The response that reaches it still finishes, and running subagents keep spending until they stop. Anthropic says to leave headroom.
  • Subagent spend counts toward the cap. After the cap is reached, starting another subagent fails with Budget limit reached, and background subagents are stopped (source).
  • When you continue a run with --continue or --resume, the totals from earlier runs don't count toward the new cap.

Output tokens and context

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS sets the maximum output for most requests. Defaults and caps depend on the model, and raising it reduces the effective context window available before auto-compaction. If a long file write ends with stop_reason: max_tokens, this setting is the place to look.

Long runs also fill up the context window. When it gets close to the limit, Claude Code summarizes older history, so instructions from early in the conversation may not be kept. If a long job seems to "forget" its rules partway through, that is often why. Put rules that must always apply in CLAUDE.md, or, with --bare, in --append-system-prompt-file. Keep tool output small: Bash output read back into context is capped by BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH (default 30,000 characters) (source).

Trigger 2: Session and tool timeouts

Several timers apply to a headless run:

TimerDefaultWhat happensSetting
Foreground Bash command2 minCommand times outBASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS
Max Bash timeout Claude can request10 minCeiling for long commandsBASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS
Idle wait for background work after the final turn10 minRunning work is stopped and its partial result droppedCLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS (0 = no cap)
Monitor watch5 minWatch times outHeadless docs
MCP server startup with --mcp-config30 sRun starts without the pending serverMCP_TIMEOUT
API request10 minRequest failsAPI_TIMEOUT_MS

Some details matter here:

  • Bare mode: with --bare, no background tasks run, so a command that reaches its timeout stops instead of moving to the background. This affects long test suites or builds.
  • Missing MCP servers don't fail the run. Claude Code skips invalid --mcp-config entries and the run continues and exits cleanly. When stderr is captured (as in CI), it prints no warning. The skipped entries only appear in mcp_server_errors in the system/init event. A CI gate can check whether that array is empty.
  • Your own scheduler can stop the run. If a CI runner or process supervisor sends SIGTERM, Claude Code exits with code 143 and records no result for the unfinished turn. To end the turn cleanly, send SIGINT first. To continue the interrupted turn when you resume, set CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN=1 (source).
  • Large piped input fails. Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. For bigger inputs, write them to a file and put the file path in the prompt.

Credentials expire too

Login expiry is not a timeout setting, but on a schedule it has the same effect. Once a /login session expires, each model request fails with Login expired. For scripts, claude setup-token creates a one-year OAuth token that you set as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. However, bare mode does not read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. With --bare, use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper instead. Also note that in -p mode, a set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is always used when present. An old key left in your shell environment will therefore override your subscription login.

Trigger 3: Permission prompts with no one to answer

This trigger causes the most confusion. In an interactive session, Claude asks and waits for you. In a headless run, what happens depends on whether there is a "permission host":

  • No host (plain claude -p): any request that would show a prompt is denied. Claude gets a rejection message and usually tries something else or reports that it couldn't continue. From outside, the job looks like it quit early.
  • With a host (an SDK canUseTool callback or --permission-prompt-tool): the run waits for that host to answer each request. If the host is not answering, the run can wait until a timer ends it.

For unattended jobs, pass --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259 or later). Anything that would prompt is denied unless a PermissionRequest hook allows it, and Claude is told not to retry.

Set the permission mode explicitly

If nothing sets a permission mode, the run uses the built-in starting mode, which can be auto. Choose the mode yourself:

ModeRuns without askingGood fit for headless
dontAskPre-approved tools, reads in working dirs, read-only commands; everything else deniedLocked-down recurring jobs
acceptEditsFile edits plus mkdir, touch, mv, cp; other shell commands still need allow rulesLint or formatting fixers
autoA classifier reviews each action (source)Broader tasks where you still want guardrails
bypassPermissionsAll tools except explicit ask rules and similar exceptions. Can't run as root on Unix; only for isolated environmentsThrowaway containers only

Allow-rule mistakes that lead to denials

  • **Missing space before *.** Bash(git diff ) matches commands starting with git diff. Without the space, Bash(git diff) would also match git diff-index.
  • Bare Bash in auto mode. In a run that starts in auto mode, a bare Bash entry is dropped and the classifier evaluates each command instead.
  • Tools that dontAsk always denies. AskUserQuestion, MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction and reads from network paths are denied even when an allow rule matches. If your prompt tells Claude to "ask me if unsure", that question will be denied in a headless run.

One more thing: without --bare, a -p run executes the hooks in the project's .claude/settings.json and connects its .mcp.json servers, even in an untrusted folder. That can change how a job behaves from one machine to another. Anthropic recommends --bare for scripted calls and says it will become the default for -p.

A prevention checklist

Here is an example nightly job that applies the points above. Adjust the paths, tools and numbers for your own job.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: nightly dependency check (illustrative values)
export BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS=600000     # long test suites
export CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=900000

claude --bare -p "Update dependency pins and run the tests" \
  --append-system-prompt-file ./agent-rules.md \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --permission-prompts none \
  --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *),Bash(npm install *),Bash(git diff *)" \
  --max-turns 40 \
  --max-budget-usd 3.00 \
  --output-format json > run.json
code=$?

subtype=$(jq -r '.subtype' run.json)
[ "$code" -ne 0 ] || [ "$subtype" != "success" ] && echo "Agent stopped: $subtype (exit $code)" >&2

Go through this list before you schedule a job:

Budgets

  • [ ] --max-turns is set with headroom, and error_max_turns triggers a resume or an alert.
  • [ ] --max-budget-usd is set a bit below your real limit, since spend can go past it.
  • [ ] Permanent rules live in CLAUDE.md or --append-system-prompt-file, not only in the opening prompt, so compaction doesn't drop them.
  • [ ] Noisy commands are piped through tail or grep so they don't fill the context window.

Timeouts

  • [ ] BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS / BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS are longer than your slowest build or test command.
  • [ ] CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS fits jobs that use background subagents.
  • [ ] The CI or job timeout is longer than the agent's own limits, and it sends SIGINT before SIGTERM.
  • [ ] Your gate fails when mcp_server_errors is not empty.
  • [ ] Authentication matches the mode: API key or apiKeyHelper with --bare, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN without it. You have a reminder before the one-year token expires.

Permissions

  • [ ] The permission mode is set explicitly (dontAsk is a sensible default).
  • [ ] --permission-prompts none is set so nothing waits on a host.
  • [ ] Every command the task needs is in --allowedTools, with correct * spacing.
  • [ ] The prompt never asks Claude to check with a human.
  • [ ] The script logs permission_denials after each run, and you add allow rules (or narrow the task) based on what it shows.

When to raise a limit and when to narrow the task

If a job keeps hitting error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd, raising the limit is not always the answer. A reasonable rule: if the turns are spent on useful work and the result is close to done, raise the limit. If the transcript shows repeated retries, denied tools or the same files being read again and again, narrow the task instead. Split it into smaller runs, hand subtasks to subagents (which start with a fresh context and only return a summary), or lower effort for routine steps. Shorter jobs with fixed limits and checked results are easier to run without supervision than one long open-ended job.
